patterns.name: Arrays & hashing
patterns.blurb: Trade memory for time: a hash map turns a second pass into a lookup.

subs.name: One pass, a few trackers
subs.about: Walk the array or string once, keeping a handful of values such as the best so far, a streak, or the previous item.

subs.name: Is it there? Sets and marks
subs.about: Remember what you have seen in a set, or mark it inside the array itself, so checking if something exists is instant.

subs.name: Count how often
subs.about: Tally how many times each value or letter appears, then answer the question from those counts.

subs.name: Group and translate by key
subs.about: Store something under a chosen key, like sorted letters or a first position, to group items or translate one into another.

subs.name: Running totals
subs.about: Keep a sum that grows as you walk, so the total of any stretch, or of each side of a point, comes from a quick subtraction.

subs.name: Look up the partner
subs.about: For each item, work out the exact value that would complete it and check a map of earlier items, including earlier running totals.

subs.name: Build a small tool
subs.about: Write a class or function others will call, choosing what to store so every call stays quick.

subs.name: Sort first, or search text
subs.about: A few problems solved by sorting before scanning, or by finding one string inside another, often a doubled copy.

big.idea: Remember what you have already seen in a lookup table, so each new item gets one quick check instead of a search.
useWhen: For each item you ask whether a matching item came earlier
You count how often things appear, or group items that share something
The slow way compares every item with every other item
big.notWhen: If the list is sorted and you may use no extra memory, a pair is found by two ends walking inward, with no table: use Two pointers.
big.realWorld: Storing API records in an object keyed by id, so a component finds any record by its id instead of searching an array.
big.cost: One pass over the data, plus memory for everything you store.

patterns.name: Two pointers
patterns.blurb: Two indexes moving through sorted or symmetric data replace a nested loop.

subs.name: Swap from both ends
subs.about: One pointer at each end walks toward the middle, to reverse things or check that a string reads the same both ways.

subs.name: Reader and writer
subs.about: One pointer reads every item and a slower one writes the keepers, so you rearrange or clean an array in place.

subs.name: One pointer per input
subs.about: Walk two lists or strings side by side, each with its own pointer, to merge, compare or match them.

subs.name: Squeeze toward a pair
subs.about: Start at both ends and drop whichever end can no longer be part of the best pair, one step at a time.

subs.name: Count pairs by squeezing
subs.about: When the two ends fit, every value between them fits too, so you count a whole batch of pairs in one step.

subs.name: Fix one, squeeze the rest
subs.about: For triples or quads, fix the first value in a loop, then find the remaining ones with a two-end squeeze.

subs.name: Runs, slopes and gaps
subs.about: Mark where each run, climb or gap starts and ends, then jump the pointer to the end and handle the next one.

subs.name: Other pointer tricks
subs.about: Pointers that walk outward from a start spot, pivot-and-reverse for the next ordering, and racing candidate starts.

big.idea: Put two fingers in the data and move them by a simple rule, so one walk replaces checking every pair.
useWhen: The list is sorted and you want two or three values that meet a target
You compare a sequence from both ends, like checking it reads the same backwards
You must clean or rearrange an array in place, without a second copy
big.notWhen: If values arrive one at a time and you must react the moment a pair fits, there are no two ends to squeeze: use a lookup table (Arrays & hashing).
big.realWorld: Merging two lists already sorted by date, such as cached and freshly fetched messages, into one timeline with one finger in each.
big.cost: One walk and almost no extra memory; sorting first, if needed, costs more.

patterns.name: Sliding window
patterns.blurb: Grow and shrink a contiguous range while keeping a summary of what is inside it.

subs.name: Running counts
subs.about: Carry one number along as you scan, such as the current run length or the lowest price so far, and reset it when the run breaks.

subs.name: Fixed-size window
subs.about: A window of exactly k items slides one step: add the item coming in, subtract the one leaving, no full re-sum.

subs.name: Fixed window with counts
subs.about: Slide a window of set length while a count map tracks which values are inside, to spot repeats or shuffled copies.

subs.name: Grow and shrink
subs.about: Extend the right edge every step and pull the left edge in only when the window breaks a rule, to find the longest or shortest fit.

subs.name: Window over sorted values
subs.about: Sort first, so values that belong together sit side by side, then slide a window over the sorted list.

subs.name: Counting windows
subs.about: Count every valid slice, not just the best one: each right edge adds a batch of good starts in one step.

subs.name: Window with a deque
subs.about: A double-ended queue keeps only the items that could still be the window's max or min, so you read it in one step.

subs.name: Streams and time windows
subs.about: Classes that take values or timestamps one at a time and forget the ones that have fallen out of the recent window.

big.idea: Frame a stretch of neighbours and slide it: add what comes in, drop what leaves, and never recount the middle.
useWhen: The answer is a run of neighbours: days in a row, characters, log lines
You want the longest, shortest or best stretch that obeys a rule
The statement says "k in a row" or "in the last 10 minutes"
big.notWhen: If the items you pick do not have to sit next to each other, there is no window; to keep the best k from anywhere, sort or use Heap / priority queue.
big.realWorld: Rate limiting: count a user's requests in the last 60 seconds and forget timestamps as they fall out of that minute.
big.cost: Each item enters and leaves the window once, plus a little memory for the window.

patterns.name: Stack
patterns.blurb: Last in, first out: matching pairs, undo, and the next greater element.

subs.name: Match brackets
subs.about: Push each opener and let a closer match the most recent one still open; often a simple depth counter is enough.

subs.name: Cancel with the top
subs.about: A new item can only cancel the last survivor, so keep survivors on a stack and pop when they cancel.

subs.name: Simulate with a stack
subs.about: Replay a process where the newest thing acts first: folders, undo steps, nested calls or colliding objects.

subs.name: Build tools from stacks
subs.about: Design small classes (history, editor, queue, min tracker, iterator) whose operations are pushes and pops.

subs.name: Evaluate and unpack nesting
subs.about: Compute expressions and nested text by saving the outer state on a stack when a bracket opens and folding it back on close.

subs.name: Next bigger or smaller
subs.about: Keep a stack sorted by value; a new item pops every waiting item it answers, finding each one's next bigger or smaller.

subs.name: Build the smallest sequence
subs.about: Build the answer on a stack and pop bigger items while it is still safe, so small values move to the front.

subs.name: Areas and contributions
subs.about: Find how far each value reaches left and right before a smaller one, then use those spans for areas or sums.

big.idea: Keep a pile where you only touch the top, so the latest unfinished thing is always the one you deal with next.
useWhen: Things open and close in nested pairs: brackets, HTML tags, folders
The newest item is the first one handled or cancelled
For each item you want the nearest bigger or smaller item after it
big.notWhen: If you must take out the smallest item, not the newest, a pile cannot reach it: use Heap / priority queue.
big.realWorld: Undo in an editor: every change goes on a pile, and Undo takes the latest one off.
big.cost: Each item goes on once and comes off at most once: one pass, plus room for the pile.

patterns.name: Binary search
patterns.blurb: Halve the search space each step, on sorted data or on the answer itself.

subs.name: Find a value or boundary
subs.about: Halve a sorted list to find a value, or the first spot where values reach a target, in a few steps.

subs.name: Search a number by its square
subs.about: Guess a whole number, square it or plug it into a formula, and keep the half where the true answer must lie.

subs.name: Sort once, search many times
subs.about: Keep a sorted list (prices, positions, saved history) and answer each query with one quick search into it.

subs.name: Pick the half by a local test
subs.about: The list is not fully sorted, but comparing the middle with a neighbour or an end still tells you which half to keep.

subs.name: Sorted grids
subs.about: Rows and columns are sorted, so you search the grid as one long list or walk a staircase from a corner.

subs.name: Binary search on the answer
subs.about: Guess the answer, check with a quick pass if it works, and halve the range: if a value works, every bigger one does too.

subs.name: K-th value by counting
subs.about: To find the k-th smallest value, guess a value, count how many items are at most it, and adjust the guess.

subs.name: Counting with sorted structures
subs.about: Merge sort, a Fenwick tree or a segment tree count or find neighbours among values seen so far, faster than checking pairs.

big.idea: Check the middle, throw away the half that cannot hold the answer, and repeat until one spot is left.
useWhen: The data is sorted and you need a value, or the first spot past some limit
You want the smallest setting that works, and anything bigger than a working setting also works
The same sorted list answers many lookups, so each one must be quick
big.notWhen: If the data is unsorted and you search it only once, sorting first costs more than one plain walk through it.
big.realWorld: git bisect: mark one good and one bad commit, test the middle one, and halve the range until the commit that broke things is found.
big.cost: Very few steps: about 20 checks find a spot among a million sorted items.

patterns.name: Linked list
patterns.blurb: Pointer surgery: reverse, merge, find the middle, detect cycles.

subs.name: One walk with a running value
subs.about: Step through the list once while carrying something along, like a number being read or a carry digit.

subs.name: Unlink and relink nodes
subs.about: Remove or move nodes by changing next pointers; a dummy node in front saves special cases for the head.

subs.name: Reverse the links
subs.about: Turn pointers around so a whole list, one stretch, or every small group runs backwards.

subs.name: Two pointers, different speeds
subs.about: Move one pointer faster or further ahead than another to find the middle or a spot near the end.

subs.name: Find a loop
subs.about: A fast and a slow pointer meet only if the chain loops; a second walk then finds where the loop starts.

subs.name: Merge sorted chains
subs.about: Join sorted lists by always taking the smaller front node, and use that to sort a list too.

subs.name: Build structures on lists
subs.about: Design caches and containers where linked nodes give quick moves, inserts and removals.

big.idea: A chain of nodes where each one knows only the next, so you change the order by rewiring links, not by moving items.
useWhen: You must reverse, split or join a chain without copying it
Items are added or removed in the middle often, and you already hold the node
You need the middle, or the k-th item from the end, in one walk
big.notWhen: If you often jump straight to item 500, a chain has to walk there node by node; a plain array (Arrays & hashing) gets there in one step.
big.realWorld: A least-recently-used cache: a lookup table finds a node, and a chain linked both ways moves it to the front without shifting anything.
big.cost: Walking costs one step per node; relinking a node you already hold takes a few steps.

patterns.name: Trees
patterns.blurb: Recursion on left and right subtrees, depth-first and level by level.

subs.name: Visit every node
subs.about: Walk the whole tree with a short recursive function, in pre-, in- or post-order, and combine what you find.

subs.name: Compare two trees side by side
subs.about: Walk two trees, or two halves of one tree, in step and check or merge the matching nodes.

subs.name: Carry a value down the path
subs.about: Pass something from the root toward the leaves, like a running sum or the largest value seen so far.

subs.name: Level by level
subs.about: Use a queue to handle the tree one row at a time, for per-level answers, views and column layouts.

subs.name: Build the answer from below
subs.about: Each node asks its children for a result first, then combines them, often recording a best answer on the side.

subs.name: Use the search-tree order
subs.about: In a search tree smaller values go left and larger go right, so you can walk one path or read values sorted.

subs.name: Ancestors and distance
subs.about: Find where two nodes' paths meet, or treat the tree as a map and measure how far nodes are from each other.

subs.name: Build, reshape and save trees
subs.about: Create a tree from lists or text, turn it back into text, or rearrange its links into a new shape.

big.idea: Data that branches like a family tree, handled by solving each branch the same way and combining the answers.
useWhen: The data is nested: each item has children, which have children of their own
A parent's answer comes from its children's answers, or a value passes down from the top
You need the data row by row, like each level of an org chart
big.notWhen: If items can point back to earlier ones or have several parents, it is not a tree and plain recursion can loop forever: use Graphs and mark visited items.
big.realWorld: A nested comment thread: a component draws one comment, then draws itself again for each reply.
big.cost: Each node is visited once; recursion also needs memory for how deep the tree goes.

patterns.name: Tries
patterns.blurb: A tree of characters for prefix lookups.

subs.name: Build a letter tree
subs.about: Store words letter by letter in shared nodes, so lookups and prefix checks walk one short path.

subs.name: Folders as a tree
subs.about: Split paths at the slashes and store each folder name as a node, so nesting and parents are easy to check.

subs.name: Search and rank with a tree
subs.about: Walk the tree alongside another search, or keep counts and top picks in each node to answer fast.

big.idea: Store words letter by letter in a shared tree, so all words that start the same way share one path.
useWhen: Many lookups ask which stored words start with the letters typed so far
Keys come in parts, like folders in a path, and many keys share their first parts
You walk a grid or text letter by letter and want to stop once no stored word starts that way
big.notWhen: If you only ask whether a whole word exists, never by its start, a Set is simpler and just as quick: use Arrays & hashing.
big.realWorld: Many URL routers store routes as a tree of path parts, so /users/42/posts follows one branch instead of testing every route.
big.cost: One step per letter of the word, however many words are stored; nodes use extra memory.

patterns.name: Heap / priority queue
patterns.blurb: Always know the smallest or largest item: top k, streaming medians, scheduling.

subs.name: Always take the top
subs.about: Keep items in a heap and repeatedly pull out the biggest or smallest, instead of scanning every time.

subs.name: Keep only the best k
subs.about: Hold just k items in a heap with the weakest on top, so it is easy to throw out when a better one arrives.

subs.name: Merge sorted lists with a heap
subs.about: Put the front of each sorted list in a heap; pop the smallest and push the next item from its list.

subs.name: Two heaps facing each other
subs.about: Split values between a max-heap and a min-heap, so both the middle or both best offers stay in reach.

subs.name: Process events in time order
subs.about: Move a clock forward and use a heap to pick which waiting job, room or building matters right now.

subs.name: Sort by one key, heap the other
subs.about: Sort by one property, then sweep while a heap keeps the best choices for the other property.

subs.name: Take now, undo the worst later
subs.about: Accept every choice for now, and when the budget runs out, use a heap to undo the one that cost most.

subs.name: Skip stale entries later
subs.about: Leave outdated entries in the heap and discard them only when they reach the top, instead of searching.

big.idea: Hold items so the smallest (or largest) is always on top, and the order repairs itself quickly after each add or removal.
useWhen: You keep needing the smallest or largest item left, while new items keep arriving
You want the top k from a long list or an endless stream
Jobs must be handled by priority or due time, not in the order they came
big.notWhen: If you need the item closest to a given value, not just the smallest, a heap cannot find it; keep a sorted list and use Binary search.
big.realWorld: A queue of timers or retry jobs where the one due soonest always runs next, however many are waiting.
big.cost: Reading the top is instant; adding or removing takes a few steps, even with millions.

patterns.name: Backtracking
patterns.blurb: Build candidates step by step and undo the step when it cannot lead to an answer.

subs.name: Subsets and combinations
subs.about: Decide for each item whether to take it, only moving forward so the same group is never built twice.

subs.name: One choice per slot
subs.about: Each position has its own short list of options; try every option at each position in turn.

subs.name: Orderings
subs.about: Fill positions one by one with items not used yet, marking them on the way in and freeing them on the way out.

subs.name: Cut a string into pieces
subs.about: Choose where the next piece ends, check that piece is valid, then solve the rest of the string the same way.

subs.name: Paths on grids and trees
subs.about: Walk step by step through cells or nodes, mark where you have been, and unmark it when you back up.

subs.name: Place pieces under rules
subs.about: Put pieces on a board one at a time, keeping quick checks of which spots are still allowed.

subs.name: Fill equal groups
subs.about: Drop items into groups that must reach the same total, biggest first, and give up early on a group that overflows.

subs.name: Search over game states
subs.about: Each move changes the whole state; try moves, cut useless ones, and remember states you already solved.

big.idea: Try choices one at a time, go deeper while they still make sense, and step back to the next choice when one leads nowhere.
useWhen: You must list every combination, ordering or arrangement
The answer is built piece by piece, and a half-built answer can already break a rule
The statement says "all possible" or "every way" and the input is small
big.notWhen: If you only need how many ways there are, or the best one, and the same smaller question keeps coming back, solve each once with 1-D dynamic programming.
big.realWorld: A simple timetable builder that places one class at a time and takes a placement back when it clashes with a rule.
big.cost: Can grow huge as the input grows; dropping dead ends early is what keeps it usable.

patterns.name: Graphs
patterns.blurb: BFS, DFS, union-find and topological order on grids and networks.

subs.name: Build the graph, then explore
subs.about: Turn the input into a list of neighbours, then count links or walk from a start to see what you can reach and how many groups exist.

subs.name: Flood fill on a grid
subs.about: Spread from a cell to the cells touching it, to measure, count, repaint or mark regions of a grid, sometimes starting from the border.

subs.name: Fewest steps with BFS
subs.about: Search one layer at a time, so the first time you reach the goal uses the fewest moves; nodes can be cells, words or puzzle states.

subs.name: Spread from many starts at once
subs.about: Put every starting cell in the queue together, so each cell learns its distance to the nearest start in one pass.

subs.name: Order by dependencies
subs.about: Arrows mean one thing must come before another; repeatedly take what is ready to get an order, levels, or proof of a loop.

subs.name: Merge groups with union-find
subs.about: Keep a parent link per item and merge groups as connections arrive, so asking whether two items are joined is almost free.

subs.name: Loops and two teams
subs.about: Spot loops, edges whose loss splits the graph, and whether nodes can be split into two sides with every edge going across.

subs.name: Trees as graphs
subs.about: A connected graph with no loops: find its longest path or its centre by peeling leaves, or reuse one answer to get every root's answer.

big.idea: Model things and the links between them as dots and lines, then explore from a start to see what connects to what.
useWhen: Things link to other things: people, cells on a grid, tasks that need other tasks first
You need the fewest moves from one state to another, and every move counts the same
You must find groups, loops, or an order that respects "A before B"
big.notWhen: If links have different costs, like minutes or fares, fewest steps is not cheapest: use Advanced graphs for weighted routes.
big.realWorld: Working out build order in a monorepo, where each package must be built after the packages it depends on, and spotting circular imports.
big.cost: Each dot and line is handled about once, plus memory to mark what you have visited.

patterns.name: Advanced graphs
patterns.blurb: Shortest paths with weights and minimum spanning trees.

subs.name: Cheapest route on weighted edges
subs.about: Edges have costs, so always grow the cheapest route found so far, sometimes carrying an extra count like stops used.

subs.name: Cheapest links first
subs.about: Join points using the smallest costs first, to connect everything cheaply or to keep the worst single step as small as possible.

subs.name: Orders and tours
subs.about: Turn rules into arrows, then find an order that respects them all or a walk that uses every arrow exactly once.

big.idea: When links have costs, always extend the cheapest route found so far, or join points with the cheapest links first.
useWhen: Links carry different costs, like minutes, fares or distance, and you want the cheapest route
You must connect every point while paying the least in total for the links
A route has an extra limit, like at most k stops
big.notWhen: If every link costs the same, the level-by-level search from Graphs finds the fewest steps more simply and faster.
big.realWorld: Route planning in a delivery app, where roads are links weighted by travel time and the quickest route is wanted.
big.cost: A bit more than a plain graph walk: each step asks a heap for the cheapest open route.

patterns.name: 1-D dynamic programming
patterns.blurb: Answer for i built from answers for smaller i.

subs.name: Build from the last few answers
subs.about: Each answer is a small sum or minimum of the few answers just before it, so fill a list left to right or keep only a couple of numbers.

subs.name: Take or skip neighbours
subs.about: At each spot either take it and skip its neighbour, or pass it by; keep the best total for both choices.

subs.name: Best ending at this spot
subs.about: Track the best slice or count that ends exactly at the current element, then extend it by one element at a time.

subs.name: A few states per step
subs.about: Keep one best value for each situation you could be in, like holding or not holding a share, and move between them each step.

subs.name: Reach an exact amount
subs.about: Fill a table for every total from 0 up to the target, building each one from smaller totals using one coin, square or part.

subs.name: Cut into valid pieces
subs.about: Decide where the last piece of a string or array starts, often with palindromes, and reuse the best answer for what came before it.

subs.name: Longest rising chain
subs.about: For each element, find the longest chain of earlier elements it can extend, then speed it up with sorting or binary search.

subs.name: Pick non-overlapping ranges
subs.about: Sort ranges by where they end and choose which to keep so none overlap, jumping back to the last range that still fits.

big.idea: Answer a question for size n by reusing stored answers for smaller sizes, so nothing is worked out twice.
useWhen: You are asked for a number of ways, or a best total, rather than every option listed
The answer at each step depends on answers at earlier steps
A try-everything recursive solution keeps asking the same smaller question
big.notWhen: If one locally best choice is provably always safe, a table is extra work; just take that choice at each step with Greedy.
big.realWorld: Balanced line breaking for a paragraph: the best layout up to each word is built from the best layouts ending at earlier words.
big.cost: One stored answer per size, each worked out once instead of over and over.

patterns.name: 2-D dynamic programming
patterns.blurb: Tables over two indexes: two strings, a grid, items and capacity.

subs.name: Walk a grid
subs.about: Each cell's answer comes from the cells above and to the left, so fill the grid row by row, often keeping just one row.

subs.name: Compare two strings
subs.about: Fill a table over every pair of prefixes of two strings to match, align, edit or count ways one fits the other.

subs.name: Count picks item by item
subs.about: Go through the items one at a time and keep a count for every running total or state the picks so far could have reached.

subs.name: Track uses left or current state
subs.about: Add a second index for how many trades, events or days are left, or for being in a hold or rest state, and fill it day by day.

subs.name: Chains keyed by the last step
subs.about: A chain's next element depends on the last gap or last two values, so store the best chain for each end and last step.

subs.name: Solve every range
subs.about: Answer each slice from i to j using smaller slices inside it, trying every split point or every choice at its two ends.

subs.name: Several things in one state
subs.about: The state holds two walkers, a whole column of colours or a shopping list, so remember the answer for each such combination.

big.idea: The same reuse idea with two things changing at once, so stored answers fill a grid: two strings, a map, items against a budget.
useWhen: Two strings or lists must be compared, lined up or edited into each other
You move across a grid only right or down and want the best route or the number of routes
Each item is taken or left, under a limit like weight, money or days
big.notWhen: If you only ask whether one string's letters appear in order inside another, no table is needed: walk both with Two pointers.
big.realWorld: A diff view: line up the old and new text by the longest part they share, so unchanged lines stay put and only real edits are marked.
big.cost: One stored answer per pair of positions; often only the last row needs keeping.

patterns.name: Greedy
patterns.blurb: Take the locally best step when you can prove it never hurts.

subs.name: Make the obvious move
subs.about: Spot the one rule that is always safe (count, take the best, fix the first problem) and apply it directly.

subs.name: Carry a running value
subs.about: Walk once from left to right, carrying one number such as the lowest so far or the current sum, and decide at each step.

subs.name: Sort, then take
subs.about: Sort the input first; then the best picks or pairings sit next to each other or at the two ends.

subs.name: Win the leftmost digit
subs.about: For the biggest or smallest number, improve the leftmost digit you can, since it outweighs all digits after it.

subs.name: Stretch the reach
subs.about: Track the farthest point you can reach so far and only commit to a step, jump or cut when you must.

subs.name: Sort by a clever key
subs.about: Find the right order to process items (a difference, a comparison, a slack) and prove swapping two items never helps.

subs.name: Scan backwards or both ways
subs.about: Some rules only settle from the right, or need one pass each way whose results you then combine.

subs.name: Grab the best with a heap
subs.about: Keep candidates in a heap or stack so the best choice at each moment is ready to take without rescanning.

big.idea: Make the choice that looks best right now and never revisit it, which works only when you can show it never hurts later.
useWhen: After sorting by the right key, the best picks seem to fall in line
One choice is always safe: the earliest finish, the lightest item, the farthest reach
big.notWhen: When the pick that looks best now can block a better total later (coins 1, 3, 4 making 6: 4+1+1 loses to 3+3), use 1-D dynamic programming.
big.realWorld: A toolbar that keeps adding buttons while they fit and moves the rest into a "More" menu.
big.cost: Usually a sort, then one pass: fast, with little extra memory.

patterns.name: Intervals
patterns.blurb: Sort by start or end, then merge, insert or count overlaps.

subs.name: Sort and merge
subs.about: Sort ranges by start, then walk once: each range either extends the block you are building or starts a new one.

subs.name: Walk calendars together
subs.about: Step through two or more sorted lists side by side, always moving past the range that ends first.

subs.name: Keep the one that ends first
subs.about: To keep the most ranges or cover them with the fewest points, sort by end and always pick the earliest finisher.

subs.name: Count overlaps with events
subs.about: Turn each range into a start and an end event, sweep them in order and keep a running count of what is open.

subs.name: Look up in a sorted timeline
subs.about: Keep ranges sorted and use binary search to find the few neighbours a new range can touch.

big.idea: Sort ranges by where they start or end, then walk them once, merging, counting or choosing as you go.
useWhen: Each item has a start and an end: bookings, shifts, time slots
You must find overlaps, merge busy times, or count the most going on at once
A new range must slot into a schedule that is already in order
big.notWhen: If ranges carry values and you want the most valuable set with no overlaps, earliest-end-first can fail: use 1-D dynamic programming.
big.realWorld: A calendar's day view that works out which events overlap and places them side by side in columns.
big.cost: Sorting is the main cost; the walk after it is a single pass.

patterns.name: Math & geometry
patterns.blurb: Matrix walks, number tricks and careful arithmetic.

subs.name: Peel off digits
subs.about: Take a number apart digit by digit with % 10 and integer division, then sum, compare or rebuild them.

subs.name: Long arithmetic with carries
subs.about: Add, multiply or divide numbers too big for normal types, column by column like on paper, passing a carry along.

subs.name: Bases, dates and text formats
subs.about: Convert between number bases, read and write numbers as text, and turn dates into day counts.

subs.name: Walk and transform grids
subs.about: Move through a 2-D grid by index: rotate, mirror, spiral, read diagonals, or update cells from their neighbours.

subs.name: Points, shapes and distances
subs.about: Work with coordinates: distances, overlapping rectangles, angles, triangles and points on a line.

subs.name: Find the formula
subs.about: Spot a pattern, sum formula or parity rule that replaces a slow step-by-step simulation with one calculation.

subs.name: Divisors, primes and gcd
subs.about: Find divisors in pairs up to the square root, sieve primes, and use the greatest common divisor to simplify.

subs.name: Fast powers, counting and chance
subs.about: Raise to big powers by squaring, keep only remainders, count arrangements by blocks, and make fair random choices.

big.idea: Problems that turn on numbers and positions: digits, remainders, primes, coordinates and grid turns, done with careful arithmetic.
useWhen: The input is a number to take apart, or one too big for normal numbers
You must rotate, mirror or spiral through a grid by its row and column indexes
A simulation would take billions of steps, but the result follows a pattern or formula
big.notWhen: If a grid question asks which cells connect, or how many moves it takes around walls, it is not arithmetic: use Graphs.
big.realWorld: A date picker that works out which weekday the 1st falls on and how many days the month has, leap years included.
big.cost: Often one quick calculation; the care goes into rounding and numbers too big to be exact.

patterns.name: Bit manipulation
patterns.blurb: XOR, masks and shifts to count, toggle and cancel out.

subs.name: Read, mask and shift bits
subs.about: Look at single bits with AND and shifts, and build masks that pick out or flip exactly the bits you want.

subs.name: Count the one bits
subs.about: Count how many bits are 1, often by repeatedly removing the lowest 1 with n & (n - 1).

subs.name: XOR cancels pairs
subs.about: A value XORed with itself is 0, so XOR a whole list and matching pairs vanish, leaving the odd one out.

subs.name: Arithmetic one bit at a time
subs.about: Add, divide or check remainders the way hardware does: column by column with a carry, or by doubling.

subs.name: Reason about each bit position
subs.about: Bits do not affect each other under OR and XOR, so solve the problem separately for each bit position.

subs.name: Doubling sequences and bit counts
subs.about: Sequences that double each round can be traced back through the binary digits of the position.

big.idea: Treat a number as a row of on/off switches and use AND, OR, XOR and shifts to read, flip or cancel them.
useWhen: Every value appears twice except one, and you must find it with no extra memory
A set of yes/no flags, like permissions or chosen items, fits inside one number
You must count, test or toggle single bits of a number
big.notWhen: With more than 32 flags, JavaScript's bit operators cut numbers to 32 bits; use a Set from Arrays & hashing, or BigInt.
big.realWorld: Permission flags kept in one number, where read, write and delete are separate bits checked with AND.
big.cost: Each operation is a single fast step, and many flags fit in one number.
